column3: The Hebrew says that they remained three years, with no war; BSB makes the years the subject that passed.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew names the king of Israel, asks “Do you know”, and describes remaining silent; BSB uses “who”, “Do you not know”, and “have failed to take it”.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew says to inquire “today”; BSB uses “first.”
Close to the Hebrew.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew describes a man through whom they may inquire of the LORD; BSB describes a man who can ask the LORD.
The Hebrew names a eunuch; BSB uses “official.”
The Hebrew says they were clothed in garments, without a separate adjective “royal”; BSB supplies that adjective.
Close to the Hebrew.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew uses “one mouth” and compares his word with the word of “one of them”; BSB uses “one accord” and compares his words collectively with theirs.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew leaves both the arriving man and respondent unnamed; BSB supplies Micaiah in both places.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew leaves the speaker unnamed and uses plural “masters”; BSB supplies Micaiah and uses singular “master.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew leaves the speaker unnamed; BSB supplies Micaiah.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew says “the spirit” and ends with its offer to entice him; BSB says “a spirit” and includes the LORD’s question here, which appears in the next Hebrew verse.

The Hebrew begins with the LORD asking by what means, a question BSB places in the preceding verse. It leaves the final speaker unnamed and uses singular “mouth,” where BSB supplies the LORD and uses plural “mouths.”
The Hebrew uses singular “mouth” for all the prophets; BSB uses plural “mouths.”
The Hebrew says he struck Micaiah on the cheek; BSB says “in the face.”
The Hebrew says “a room within a room”; BSB condenses this to “an inner room” and adds “soon.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew calls the provisions “bread of distress” and “water of distress”; BSB renders these as “only bread and water.”
The Hebrew addresses plural “peoples”; BSB says “all you people.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew says “your garments” without a separate adjective “royal”; BSB supplies “royal.”
